description: Trying to build a website that will actually work in the real world not js win the hackathon (tho that is an aim).
summary: We developed Cosmos Xpand, an interactive web visualization tool that enables citizens, scientists, and researchers to all sky near infrared images from NASA's SPHEREx mission. By entering the object name or coordinates, users get the imagery of the object straight from SPHEREx mission data of choosing surveys . To make faint anomalies stand out, our tool combines rapid time-lapse blink comparator with an interactive slit-screen slider and difference overlay between two surveys to pinpoint movements of the objects. Users can log their explorations while earning badges by interacting with the data. Because SPHEREx maps the entire over six months across 102 infrared bands generating images upon billions of objects. Cosmos Xpand turns complex multi-epoch FITS files into instant visual comparisons, eliminating technical barriers and make it easily accessible to scientists, while also empowering anyone to uncover hidden asteroids, comets, brown dwarfs and various other objects.
details:
Cosmos Xpand is a browser-based explorer for NASA's SPHEREx mission. SPHEREx

re-surveys the entire sky in infrared roughly every six months, so the same

patch of sky has been imaged at different moments — and comparing those moments

is how you catch something that moves or changes. That comparison normally sits

inside archive interfaces built for researchers. Our project makes it one

click: pick a spot, and see how the mission saw it, pass by pass.

It works like this. The visitor clicks anywhere on an all-sky map, or searches

an object name (resolved through CDS Sesame). The app asks IRSA which SPHEREx

observations cover that position, querying both live releases — DR1 and Quick

Release 3 — and merging the results into survey passes by date. For the chosen

pass and wavelength band it fetches the real level-2 FITS cutout, parses the

image in a Cloudflare Worker, and sends the pixel values back to the browser.

We render them ourselves: an asinh stretch, and a hue set by wavelength, so

blue sits at 0.75 micrometres and red at 5. Both frames in a comparison share

one stretch and one colour map, which means a difference on screen is a

difference in the sky, not in the display.

From there the visitor can blink or slide between two passes, step the

wavelength band by band (D1–D6), or switch to a composite of the bands covering

that position. Every location also gets a "spectral fingerprint" — aperture

photometry measured in the browser across those bands — alongside the object's

name, exact coordinates, the dates SPHEREx observed it, and the raw FITS header

of the frame on screen. Anything interesting can be saved to a personal log

with a note about what changed between passes, and that activity earns badges.

Exploring is free and needs no account; signing in only adds the log.

Tools and stack: TypeScript and React (built with Vite) for the interface; a

JavaScript Cloudflare Worker on Freebuff Sites for the archive proxies,

sign-in and per-user data; Cloudflare D1 for storage; Aladin Lite from CDS for

the full-resolution sky view; Cloudflare Workers AI for the sky guide; and

Python for the verification harness we used to prove our pixel pipeline

matches the archive's own cutouts exactly (86,165 of 86,165 pixels identical

across two releases).

The creative core is treating "the sky changes" as something you can browse

rather than query — a blink you can scrub — and rewarding discovery without

inventing data. What we deliberately refused to do was fake colour: no frame is

presented as true colour, and the site explains exactly how each hue was

chosen.

Our team weighed distributed timezones by freezing interfaces early and

working against them; scope, by showing the six bandpasses the archive

actually publishes rather than implying all 102 spectral channels; honesty

about provenance, including printing the FITS header so anyone can check us;

and the fact that the archive is a third-party dependency that sometimes goes

down — so the site caches the last good coverage and says plainly when the

archive is unavailable instead of showing an empty frame.

The intended impact is to make a science archive feel like a place to wander:

someone with no astronomy background should be able to find a moving object,

see it move, and understand why that matters.
